name: Nicanor Archibeque
equipment: Leather duster, sun-faded, with a rip down the back where a mesquite thorn caught it
Navy revolver (Colt, .36), 6 chambers loaded, in a Mexican holster his father made
Repeating rifle (Winchester 1873, .44), in a saddle scabbard
Bowie knife on his belt, and a smaller knife in his boot for cutting rawhide
Horse: Canelo, a sorrel cow pony with a white blaze, quick as a cat on the turn and afraid of nothing but pigs
A Mexican saddle with a broad horn, bridle, saddlebags, bedroll and a serape that doubles as a blanket
Reata: sixty feet of braided rawhide that he plaited himself over one winter
Spurs with big rowels, and leather chaps
A letter of reference from an Albuquerque horse buyer, in English, which he cannot quite read
A money belt with $310 from the sale of forty horses, which belongs to his mother and the family
features: Both Sides of the River (Borderlands origin: speaks Spanish and English natively, knows the fords, trails and plazas of the Rio Abajo and the borderlands, and has advantage on Persuasion and Insight checks with border people of either side; can always find a guide, a ford or a bed among them)

Saddle-Born (Cowhand: advantage on Riding checks, never disadvantage on ranged attacks from the saddle, mounts and dismounts with 5 ft of movement; his horse Canelo is part of him: +15 hit points, never spooks under him, comes to his whistle from half a mile and acts on his initiative; proficient with the lariat, and from the saddle throws a loop as a bonus action once per turn)
Rawhide (Cowhand: advantage on saving throws against exhaustion, heat and cold; rides 12 hours a day without forced-march saves; spends one extra Hit Die on a short rest)

Cow Sense (Cowhand, 2nd level: advantage on Animal Handling checks with cattle, horses and mules; turns the leaders of a stampede with a single Riding or Animal Handling check as an action, with advantage)

Outfit: Vaquero (Cowhand, 3rd level: his reata reaches 40 ft, a creature he ropes from the saddle can be thrown prone and dragged without a further check, and he can rope two targets at once as one action)

The Trail Outfit (Cattle Drover background: any trail crew, ranch, sheep camp or cow-town saloon takes him in for a night; knows the trails, crossings and horse markets from the Rio Puerco to Fort Wingate, and who in them cheats a vaquero)

personality.traits: I laugh easily, sing badly and lose my temper all at once, like a dry arroyo in a storm. I would rather be on a horse than anywhere else on earth. I call every horse by name and most people by nickname.
personality.ideals: The commons belong to everybody on the grant, the way the air does. Nobody sells the air.
personality.bonds: My little brother Tiburcio, who rides better than I do and has never had a thought in his head that he did not say out loud. My mother. My uncle Celestino, who taught me my letters and thinks I forgot them.
personality.flaws: In May I pulled up thirty of the Company surveyor's stakes at the Ojo del Gato and threw them in the spring, and I have told nobody. I do things first and think about them on the ride home.

appearance: A lean, sun-black young man of twenty-four, of middle height, with a thin moustache he is proud of, quick dark eyes and a white scar across the back of one hand from a bad rope. Flat-crowned black hat with a horsehair band, a blue cotton shirt, a red sash, leather chaps, big spurs. He sits Canelo as if he had grown there.
backstory: Nicanor Archibeque was born in 1857 on the plaza of Santa Teresita, in a family that has held the same house lot and the same strip of irrigated land on the acequia madre since one of the twenty-four founding families walked the boundaries with Ventura Lucero in 1768. His father was a vaquero of the commons and died under a horse when Nicanor was twelve, and from that day Nicanor was one too. He has ridden the commons from the Cerro Colorado to the Sierra Prieta, worked cattle for half the ranchers in the county, driven horses to the army at Fort Wingate and to buyers in Albuquerque, and taught his younger brother Tiburcio everything he knows, which was a mistake, because now Tiburcio is better at it. His mother, Doña Encarnación, is Celestino Trujillo's sister; Celestino is running for probate judge against the Company and has asked Nicanor to stop pulling up the Company's stakes before somebody shoots him. On 29 June 1881 Nicanor is riding home from Albuquerque beside the Rio Seco line's last coach, with $310 of the family's horse money in a belt under his shirt and his uncle inside the coach, lecturing the other passengers. He has no idea his brother is waiting for him at the Puerto de Piedra, holding four strangers' horses in an arroyo. (Suggested employer: the plaza, and his brother. Hooks: Tiburcio's sombrero in the arroyo; his uncle's campaign; the stakes he pulled up in May.)
